name: Deodorant

lead: Deodorant gives you a cleaner, fresher scent, which matters because smell shapes how attractive you come across up close.

Underarm bacteria break down sweat, especially apocrine secretions that become active at puberty, and that produces odor. Deodorants mask it with fragrance, absorb moisture, or inhibit bacteria with ingredients such as alcohol, triclosan or alum. They do not reduce sweating; that is what antiperspirants do. In the US they are regulated as cosmetics.

paras: Applied to clean, dry underarms as a stick, spray or roll-on, usually daily and often layered with fragrance or alongside an antiperspirant. Odor control is noticeable straight away.
Some ingredients can cause skin irritation or contact dermatitis, and aerosols held too close can cause cold burns. Ingredients such as triclosan and phthalates have been studied for exposure.

angle.text: Deodorant controls underarm odor and adds scent, the basic step for smelling clean and being more pleasant to be near. The effect on odor is noticeable straight away.

lead: A deodorant is a product applied to the skin, usually the underarms, to control body odor. It does not stop sweating, unlike an antiperspirant.[1][2] Odor arises mainly when skin bacteria break down sweat, especially apocrine secretions that become active at puberty.[1][3]

Deodorants work by masking odor with fragrance, absorbing moisture, or inhibiting bacteria with ingredients such as alcohol, triclosan or alum crystals.[1][2] In the US they are regulated as cosmetics.[1] In looksmaxxing forums, deodorant and fragrance are discussed as part of scent and hygiene.

paras: Formats include sprays, roll-ons, sticks, gels and crystal products made from potassium or ammonium alum.[1][2] Antimicrobial triclosan has been widely used in personal care products and its applications and safety were reviewed in 1996, while later work measured it in human plasma and milk.[4][5] Natural options based on essential oils or plant extracts have grown since the 2010s.[2]

Wikipedia dates the first modern commercial deodorant, Mum, to 1888 in Philadelphia, and the first commercial antiperspirant, Everdry, to 1903.[1] Roll-on applicators arrived in 1952, and aerosols dominated in the 1960s and early 1970s before the FDA's 1977 ban of an aluminium zirconium ingredient.[1]
A 2015 study mapped underarm bacteria responsible for body odor using culture-independent methods, and a 2019 study examined how skin care products affect skin chemistry and microbiome dynamics.[6]

Possible reactions include irritation from ingredients like propylene glycol and dermatitis from alum crystals.[1] Fragrance-fixing phthalates in personal care products have been linked in studies to urinary metabolite levels in women.[7] Aerosol sprays held close can cause cold burns.[1]
No studies found testing deodorant for attractiveness outcomes. Related research examines ingredient exposure and skin microbiota.[4][5][6][7]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, deodorant and fragrance come up as part of scent as a trait, with users asking which products to use and whether skipping them matters.[8][9]

claims.claim: Smell matters to how attractive you are perceived.
Skipping soap and deodorant gives an ideal natural scent after showering.
Rubbing lemon on the armpits improves scent.

timeline.event: Mum, the first modern commercial deodorant, introduced in the US.[1]
Everdry marketed as first commercial antiperspirant.[1]
